Monsoon Season Health Precautions
A Public Health Awareness Reference
Health Awareness Chatbot Knowledge Base | General Public Information Only
Overview
The monsoon season brings much-needed rain, but it also creates conditions where certain illnesses spread more easily. Heavy rain, waterlogging, and humidity allow disease-causing germs and mosquitoes to multiply quickly, while flooding can contaminate drinking water sources and food. The most common health problems during the monsoon include water-borne diseases such as diarrhoea, typhoid, and cholera, and mosquito-borne diseases such as malaria, dengue, and chikungunya. Skin infections and food poisoning also become more common in this season.

Skin infections and food poisoning also become more common in this season. Most of these illnesses can be prevented through simple precautions related to safe water, mosquito control, food safety, and general hygiene. Being aware of these risks and acting early can protect individuals, families, and entire communities during the rainy months.

Key Practices
Water-Borne Disease Prevention
Drink only clean, safe water; boil water if its safety is uncertain, especially after heavy rain or flooding
Store drinking water in a clean, covered container, and avoid drawing water with hands or unclean utensils
Avoid drinking water from open wells, ponds, or sources that may be contaminated by floodwater or overflow from drains
Wash hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet
If diarrhoea occurs, give plenty of fluids and oral rehydration solution to prevent dehydration, and seek medical care promptly, especially for children and the elderly
Mosquito Control
Do not allow water to collect or stagnate in and around the house, including in pots, tyres, coolers, and containers
Empty, clean, and dry water-storage containers regularly to stop mosquitoes from breeding
Use mosquito nets while sleeping, and use screens on doors and windows where possible
Wear full-sleeved clothing, especially during early morning and evening hours when mosquitoes are most active
Use mosquito repellents and coils as needed, particularly for children and pregnant women
Support local mosquito-control efforts such as fogging and larvicide spraying carried out by health workers
Food Safety
Eat freshly cooked, hot food, and avoid food that has been left uncovered or exposed to flies
Wash fruits and vegetables thoroughly with clean water before eating or cooking
Avoid street food and cut fruit sold in the open during the monsoon, as these are more likely to carry germs
Store cooked food properly and avoid eating leftovers that have been kept for long periods without refrigeration
Keep kitchen areas clean and free from flies, pests, and stagnant water
General Precautions
Avoid wading through floodwater where possible; wash feet and legs thoroughly with soap if contact cannot be avoided
Rest and stay hydrated if feeling unwell, and avoid self-treating fever that lasts more than two to three days
Seek medical care promptly for high fever, severe body ache, persistent vomiting, or signs of dehydration
Keep the surroundings of the home clean, and ensure proper drainage to avoid waterlogging
Why It Matters
During the monsoon, contaminated water and food become a major route for diseases like diarrhoea, typhoid, and cholera to spread within families and communities, particularly affecting young children and the elderly, who are more vulnerable to dehydration and complications.

At the same time, stagnant water created by the rains becomes an ideal breeding ground for mosquitoes that spread malaria, dengue, and chikungunya. These illnesses can cause high fever, severe body pain, and in some cases serious complications, so early recognition and prompt medical attention are important. Because many monsoon illnesses share similar symptoms, such as fever and body ache, it is important not to self-diagnose. A visit to the nearest health centre for proper testing is the safest way to identify the illness and begin the right care in time. Community-level prevention, such as controlling mosquito breeding sites and maintaining clean drainage, is often more effective than individual precautions alone, so cooperating with local health and sanitation efforts benefits everyone.

Odisha-Specific Context
Odisha's monsoon season, driven mainly by the South-West monsoon, typically brings heavy rainfall between June and September, along with the risk of cyclones, particularly in coastal areas. The state is among the more flood-prone regions of the country, and low-lying and riverine districts are especially vulnerable to waterlogging and flash floods during this period.

Coastal and riverine districts, including those along the Mahanadi and other major rivers, are more prone to flooding, waterlogging, and disruption of safe drinking water supply during heavy rains
Following floods or cyclones, health authorities in Odisha have at times issued alerts for water-borne illnesses such as diarrhoea in affected districts, along with deployment of medical teams and preventive measures
The state government works with district health teams, ASHA workers, and disaster management authorities to carry out disease surveillance, chlorination of drinking water sources, and mosquito control activities during and after the monsoon
Residents in flood-prone and low-lying areas are encouraged to store extra clean drinking water when heavy rain is forecast, keep essential medicines on hand, and know the location of the nearest health facility or emergency shelter
Following updates from local authorities, the Indian Meteorological Department, and the Odisha State Disaster Management Authority during periods of heavy rainfall or cyclone warnings can help families prepare in advance
Being prepared ahead of the monsoon and following basic precautions can greatly reduce health risks for families across Odisha's rural, coastal, and flood-prone areas.

Basic Nutrition Guidance for Families
A Public Health Awareness Reference
Health Awareness Chatbot Knowledge Base | General Public Information Only
Overview
Good nutrition means eating a variety of foods in the right amounts to keep the body healthy, active, and able to fight illness. What a family eats every day has a direct effect on the growth of children, the strength of working adults, and the health of pregnant women and elderly family members. A healthy diet does not need to be expensive or complicated. It simply means eating a balanced mix of foods, avoiding excess sugar, salt, and oil, and making the most of foods that are already available locally.

Poor nutrition, whether from eating too little or eating an unbalanced diet, can lead to problems such as poor growth in children, weakness, low immunity, and a higher risk of long-term diseases like diabetes and heart disease in adults. This document offers simple, general guidance on healthy eating for the whole family, along with information on why nutrition matters and how local food traditions can support good health.

Key Practices
Eat a Variety of Foods
Include foods from different groups at each meal: cereals (rice, wheat, millets), pulses (dal, beans), vegetables, fruits, and where possible, milk, eggs, or meat
Eat a mix of colours of fruits and vegetables, as different colours provide different vitamins and minerals
Use a combination of cereals and pulses (such as rice and dal) together, as this improves the quality of protein in the meal
Balance the Plate
Fill about half the plate with vegetables and fruits
Include a portion of whole grains such as rice, wheat, or millets
Add a portion of pulses, beans, eggs, fish, or meat for protein, based on what is available and affordable
Use oil and ghee in moderation rather than in excess
Limit Salt, Sugar, and Oil
Reduce added salt in cooking and avoid excess salty snacks, pickles, and papad
Limit sugary drinks, sweets, and packaged snacks
Choose boiled, steamed, or lightly cooked foods over deep-fried foods when possible
Special Attention for Vulnerable Groups
Young children need frequent, small meals with a variety of foods to support healthy growth
Breastfeeding is recommended for infants in the first months of life, along with timely introduction of a variety of foods as the child grows
Pregnant and breastfeeding women need extra nutritious food, including iron- and protein-rich foods, to support their own health and their child's growth
Elderly family members should be encouraged to eat soft, easily digestible, nutrient-rich foods and to stay well hydrated
General Habits
Eat meals at regular times and avoid skipping meals
Drink enough clean water through the day
Wash fruits and vegetables well before eating or cooking
Where possible, grow a small kitchen garden with vegetables and leafy greens for fresh, affordable nutrition
Why It Matters
Good nutrition supports healthy growth in children, helps prevent illness, and gives the body strength for daily work and study.

Malnutrition, whether from too little food or an unbalanced diet, can affect a child's physical growth and ability to learn, and can weaken the immune system, making infections more likely. At the same time, unhealthy eating habits, such as excess salt, sugar, and oily food, contribute to long-term health problems including high blood pressure, diabetes, and heart disease. Following a balanced diet from childhood through old age helps reduce the risk of these conditions later in life. Proper nutrition is especially important during pregnancy, early childhood, and adolescence, as these are periods of rapid growth and development. Good nutrition in these stages has a lasting impact on health across a person's lifetime.

Odisha has a rich tradition of local foods that can support good nutrition when eaten in the right balance. Everyday staples such as rice, dal, seasonal vegetables, and leafy greens form the foundation of a healthy Odia diet and are widely accessible across the state.

Traditional millets such as ragi (mandia), suan, and kangu are climate-resilient, nutrient-rich grains that have long been part of the diet in Odisha's tribal and rainfed regions

Families are encouraged to combine traditional foods like rice, dal, seasonal vegetables, and millets to create balanced, affordable, and locally accessible meals
Making the most of these local foods is an easy and culturally familiar way for Odisha families to support good nutrition at home.

Public Healthcare Facilities in Puri District, Odisha
A Structured Reference Guide to District, Community, and Primary Health Facilities
Overview
Puri district, best known as the seat of the Jagannath Temple and a major pilgrimage and coastal destination, is served by a tiered public healthcare network under the Odisha Department of Health & Family Welfare, coordinated locally by the Chief District Medical Officer (CDMO), Puri. The system follows the standard national structure: village-level Sub-Centres feed into Primary Health Centres (PHCs), which refer upward to Community Health Centres (CHCs) at the block level, which in turn refer to the District Headquarters Hospital (DHH) as the district's main secondary-level referral point.

Puri city is also home to Shri Jagannath Medical College and Hospital (SJMCH), a government medical college established in 2021, which adds a tertiary-care teaching hospital tier above the DHH. This overall structure follows the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS), issued by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) through the National Health Mission (NHM) and most recently revised in 2022. Facility Types
District Headquarters Hospital (DHH), Puri
DHH Puri, originally known as the Puri Pilgrimage Hospital, was rebuilt in 1909-10 and remains one of the district's oldest and most established public health institutions. It has the distinction of being among the first district hospitals in Odisha, and the second in India, to receive ISO 9001:2008 quality management certification.

As the district's secondary-level referral hospital, it is designed to receive cases referred from CHCs, PHCs, and Sub-Centres across all of Puri district's blocks, and given the district's high pilgrim and tourist footfall, it also plays an important role in handling visitor health emergencies alongside routine district referral care. Community Health Centres (CHCs)
CHCs are block-level referral units, generally serving a population of roughly 80,000 to 120,000 people. Puri district's blocks — including Kanas, Gop, Chandanpur/Nimapara area, Brahmagiri, Satyabadi, Astaranga, Delanga, Pipili, and others — each have a CHC that acts as the referral hub for the PHCs and Sub-Centres within that block.

For example, CHC Kanas, established in 1962, is a 24x7 facility (non-FRU) overseeing five PHCs and twenty-three Sub-Centres in its block, and is ISO 9001:2015 certified, illustrating the level of service standardization found at some CHCs in the district. A CHC is expected to have around 30 inpatient beds, an operation theatre, basic diagnostic and blood storage facilities, and specialist coverage in medicine, surgery, obstetrics/gynaecology, and paediatrics, though actual staffing varies by centre; centres equipped for round-the-clock emergency obstetric and newborn care may be designated First Referral Units (FRUs).

Primary Health Centres (PHCs)
PHCs are typically the first point of contact with a qualified doctor for rural and semi-urban residents, each covering a population of around 20,000 to 30,000. Puri district has numerous PHCs and newer PHC(New) facilities distributed across its blocks — for instance, Astaranga block alone has several PHC(New) units in addition to its main PHC. Each PHC supervises a cluster of Sub-Centres, provides outpatient consultation, a small number of inpatient beds, basic laboratory testing, and normal delivery services at PHCs designated for 24x7 care, and oversees ASHA and ANM workers at the village level.

Sub-Centres and Health & Wellness Centres
Below the PHC level, Health Sub-Centres — increasingly upgraded as Ayushman Bharat Health and Wellness Centres (AB-HWCs) — are the most peripheral public facilities, generally staffed by an ANM and a Community Health Officer. They handle preventive and promotive care such as immunization and antenatal check-ups, referring more complex cases upward to the PHC.

What Each Facility Handles
District Headquarters Hospital
Complex and emergency cases referred from CHCs and PHCs across the district
Broader specialist consultation and surgical services than block-level facilities
Diagnostics, blood storage/blood bank services, and larger inpatient bed capacity
Emergency care for pilgrims and tourists visiting Puri, alongside routine district referral cases
Possible empanelment under schemes such as Ayushman Bharat–PM-JAY for cashless treatment (current empanelment status should be verified locally)
Acts as the secondary-level referral hospital for the district, with onward referral to Shri Jagannath Medical College and Hospital or another tertiary centre for cases needing higher-level specialty care
Community Health Centres
Referral care for PHCs and Sub-Centres within the block, plus specialist consultation for patients approaching directly
Inpatient care (around 30 beds at fully staffed centres), minor and some major surgical procedures, and operation theatre services
Emergency obstetric care and institutional deliveries, particularly at 24x7-designated centres
Basic diagnostics including laboratory services and, at many centres, X-ray facilities
Primary Health Centres
Outpatient consultation for common illnesses, minor injuries, and chronic disease follow-up
Antenatal, natal, and postnatal care, including normal deliveries at 24x7 PHCs
Immunization, family planning services, and national health programme delivery (TB, malaria, non-communicable disease screening, and similar)
Basic laboratory tests (blood, urine, blood sugar, malaria rapid tests, and similar)
First-level stabilization and referral of serious cases to a CHC or the District Headquarters Hospital
How to Reach Them (General Guidance)
Since exact addresses and phone numbers are not being invented here, the following general approaches can help locate and reach the correct facility:
Ask the local ASHA worker, ANM, or Anganwadi worker — they know the nearest Sub-Centre and PHC serving a household and can help with referral upward if needed.

Every block headquarters in Puri district has a CHC (for example, Kanas, Gop, Chandanpur, Brahmagiri); the block administrative office can confirm its exact current location and status. The Puri district administration's official website and the CDMO Puri office maintain listings of health facilities; these should be treated as the authoritative source for confirmed addresses and phone numbers. The National Health Mission (NHM) Odisha and Odisha Directorate of Health Services websites publish facility directories and health scheme information at the state level. The 108 (emergency response) and 102 (patient transport / maternal-child) ambulance services can be used to reach an appropriate facility in an emergency, and can also help route a patient to the correct level of care.

For the District Headquarters Hospital specifically, and to distinguish it from Shri Jagannath Medical College and Hospital located separately in Puri city, confirm the current address and scope of services with the district health administration before travelling. Given Puri's high pilgrim and tourist traffic, visitors unfamiliar with the area should ask local authorities, hotel staff, or temple administration for the nearest functioning public health facility in an emergency.

When to Go to District Hospital vs PHC
Go to a PHC (or Sub-Centre) first for:
Routine illnesses — fever, cold, minor infections, common ailments
Antenatal check-ups, immunizations, and family planning services
Normal, uncomplicated deliveries at a 24x7-designated PHC
Basic diagnostic tests and follow-up for chronic conditions already under management
Minor injuries and first-aid level care
Go to (or be referred to) a CHC for:
Cases needing minor surgery, specialist consultation, or inpatient observation beyond what a PHC can provide
Complicated deliveries or emergency obstetric care, especially at a 24x7 or FRU-designated CHC
Situations where the PHC has stabilized a patient but recommended referral
Go directly to the District Headquarters Hospital for:
Serious emergencies — major trauma, accidents, severe medical emergencies where higher-level care is clearly needed
Conditions requiring specialist care, surgery, or diagnostics not available at PHC or CHC level
Cases already referred by a PHC or CHC as needing secondary-level hospital care
Health emergencies during pilgrimage seasons or large public gatherings, when DHH Puri is typically better equipped to handle higher patient volumes than a PHC
Situations covered under empanelled schemes (e.g., PM-JAY) requiring hospital-level admission — confirm current scheme coverage locally
As a general rule, the public health system is designed as a step-up referral chain: Sub-Centre → PHC → CHC → District Headquarters Hospital → Medical College Hospital, with each level equipped for progressively more complex care.

In Puri's case, DHH's long-established role and ISO certification make it a strong first stop for most secondary-level care, with Shri Jagannath Medical College and Hospital available for cases needing tertiary or specialized attention. Bypassing lower tiers is appropriate mainly in genuine emergencies, where reaching the nearest capable facility quickly — often via 108 ambulance services — matters more than following the tier order.
